headline: Could AI end the world? Experts disagree

chunks.text: The debate over whether AI could cause [[human extinction]] has {{flared up}} again. On September 8, a researcher at Anthropic quit. He wrote online that top labs were racing toward [[self-improving]] systems and "gambling with our lives." His posts drew 153 million views in 36 hours. A senior [[safety researcher]] there {{backed him up}}. He put the [[odds]] of AI killing all humans above 10 percent within a [[decade]].

verbs.wrong: To be settled by a formal vote
verbs.why: Old arguments flare up at every family dinner. A skin problem can flare up in hot weather. The debate over AI and human extinction flared up again after a researcher quit Anthropic.

verbs.correct: To support what someone has said
verbs.wrong: To replace someone in a job
verbs.why: My coworker backed me up when I reported the problem. The video backs up her version of events. A senior safety researcher backed up the researcher who quit, saying AI really could kill all humans.

chunks.text: The industry calls this number the "probability of doom." [[Estimates]] vary widely. The head of one leading lab puts the chance of disaster at 10 to 25 percent. One AI scientist {{points out}} that any such number is a [[wild guess]]. A 2025 [[survey]] of 272 experts {{came up with}} 21.5 percent. In 2023, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind {{put out}} a statement. It said this risk should be treated like [[pandemics]] and [[nuclear war]].

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To refuse to answer a question
verbs.why: The teacher pointed out a mistake in my essay. He pointed out that the store closes early on Sundays. One AI scientist points out that any such number is really a wild guess.

verbs.correct: To produce an answer or figure
verbs.why: The team came up with a cheaper plan. She came up with a good name for the cafe. A 2025 survey of 272 experts came up with a risk figure of 21.5 percent.

verbs.correct: To publish something for the public
verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan at the last minute
verbs.why: The company put out a short press release. The city puts out a weather warning every summer. In 2023, the heads of three major labs put out a statement comparing AI risk to pandemics and nuclear war.

chunks.text: If AI builders believe this, why do they {{carry on}}? An academic news site gave three answers on September 11. Some leaders believe the [[benefits]] will {{make up for}} the risks. Some say you cannot make AI safe without building it first. And many fear that if one lab {{slows down}}, a [[rival]] will {{catch up}} and win. In July, 1,300 lab employees signed an [[open letter]] asking the US government to help {{hold back}} the [[pace]] of development.

verbs.wrong: To move work to a new place
verbs.why: The workers carried on despite the rain. She carried on studying after the baby was born. Critics ask why the labs carry on building AI if they believe it could end humanity.

verbs.correct: To be enough to balance something bad
verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: A big bonus made up for the long hours. Nothing can make up for lost time with family. Some AI leaders believe the benefits will make up for the risks.

verbs.correct: To move or work at a lower speed
verbs.wrong: To close a company for good
verbs.why: The train slowed down before the station. Sales slow down every January. Many in the industry fear that if one lab slows down, a rival will simply win the race.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as a leader
verbs.wrong: To copy what another company makes
verbs.why: She missed a week of class and had to catch up. The smaller team caught up by the final lap. Labs fear a rival will catch up if they slow down.

verbs.correct: To stop something from moving fast
verbs.wrong: To keep a promise made earlier
verbs.why: The dam holds back the river in spring. High prices held back sales of the new phone. About 1,300 employees asked the US government to help hold back the pace of AI development.

chunks.text: On September 12, the head of Anthropic published an essay calling for a [[voluntary]] slowdown and [[independent auditors]]. Two days later, the US president {{pushed back}} against new AI rules. A rival chief executive called the plan "a [[cartel]] by any other name." A campaign for global AI "[[red lines]]" began at the United Nations in September 2025. It wants governments to {{sign off on}} an agreement by the end of 2026. That [[deadline]] is four months away.

verbs.correct: To oppose an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To hand a job to someone else
verbs.why: Parents pushed back against the longer school day. The staff pushed back when the boss cut breaks. The US president pushed back against new AI rules two days after the Anthropic essay.
The manager signed off on the new budget. The doctor must sign off on the treatment plan. The red lines campaign wants governments to sign off on an agreement by the end of 2026.

mainIdea.s: A researcher's resignation from a top AI lab has renewed the argument over whether AI could end humanity. Labs admit the risk is real, but they say stopping alone would not work.
mainIdea.why: After the resignation, labs gave three reasons for continuing, while critics and a red lines campaign ask governments to act.

mainIdea.s: After a researcher quit, the leading AI labs agreed to pause all training until governments sign a global treaty. Rival companies quickly called the pause a cartel in disguise.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no lab paused training. The head of Anthropic called for a voluntary slowdown, and one rival attacked that plan.

mainIdea.s: The United Nations has adopted a binding treaty that bans AI from designing weapons or copying humans. Leading labs say they will follow the new rules starting next year.
mainIdea.why: No treaty exists yet. A campaign wants governments to sign off on an agreement by the end of 2026.

tf.s: The Anthropic researcher's posts drew 153 million views in 36 hours.
tf.why: The posts spread fast, and a senior safety researcher backed him up soon after.

tf.s: A senior safety researcher put the odds of AI killing all humans below 1 percent.
tf.why: He backed up his colleague and put the odds above 10 percent within a decade.

tf.s: A 2025 survey of 272 experts came up with a figure of 21.5 percent.
tf.why: That figure sits between the lab head's 10 to 25 percent and the scientist who calls any number a wild guess.

tf.s: Many in the industry fear that if one lab slows down, a rival will catch up.
tf.why: That race is one of the three reasons labs carry on despite the risks they admit.

tf.s: In July, 1,300 lab employees signed an open letter asking labs to speed up.
tf.why: The letter asked the US government to help hold back the pace of development.

tf.s: The head of Anthropic pushed back against a voluntary slowdown.
tf.why: He called for a voluntary slowdown and independent auditors. It was the US president who pushed back against new rules.
